item.title: Marvellous Filters
item.description:
Marvellous filters#

Wolverine has a face that is hard to miss. But what happens when we stop thinking of it as a picture and start thinking of it as data?

In this set of assignments, we will explore images using JavaScript. We will flip them, rotate them, crop them, change their brightness, add colour, blur them, and even look for interesting patterns hidden inside them.

Our subject is Wolverine. Our tool is the bitmap.

item.title: Peaks
item.description:
Peaks#

A peak is a value that is greater than the values immediately before and after it.

Your task is to detect peaks in an array of numbers and draw a line chart that highlights them.

Reference output

Requirements#

  • Create an array of numbers yourself. Start with fixed values so you can reason about the expected output. Once your program is working, experiment with randomly generated data.
  • Draw a line chart representing the values in your array.
  • Identify peaks and highlight them with red circles.
  • A value is a peak only if it is strictly greater than both its immediate neighbours. The first and last elements cannot be peaks. Equal values and plateaus do not count as peaks.
  • Determine the horizontal and vertical scales from the data and the dimensions of the screen.
  • Scale the vertical axis so that the maximum value maps to 90% of the screen height.
  • Calculate the horizontal spacing of the data points appropriately. Each point must occupy at least one pixel horizontally. If the data exceeds the available screen width, it is truncated.
  • Allow the screen width and height to be configured.
  • Use only the following colours: r.SKYWHITE, r.BLACK, and r.RED.

Before you begin#

Resist the temptation to start writing code immediately.

item.title: Averages
item.description:
Averages#

In this assignment, you will draw a bar chart representing an array of numbers. You will also draw a horizontal line representing the average of those numbers.

Requirements#

  • The screen width and height must be configurable.
  • The width of each bar must be configurable. It must not be less than 1.
  • The gap between consecutive bars must be configurable.
  • The horizontal and vertical scales must be determined by the data.
  • The largest value in the array must correspond to 90% of the screen height. Use the same vertical scale for every value.
  • If the bars extend beyond the screen width, the excess data may be truncated.
  • Draw the bars in r.DARKBLUE.
  • Draw the average as a horizontal line in r.RED.
  • Use r.SKYWHITE for the background.

item.title: Movement and Frame Time
item.description:
Is the dinosaur always this fast?#

In the fourth part of The Long Run, we gave the dinosaur a velocity and gravity.

Your code may look different, but somewhere it probably does something like this:

dino.velocityY -= dino.gravity;
dino.y -= dino.velocityY;

The velocity changes on every update. The position changes on every update too.

This produces a jump, but there is a problem hiding in it.

item.title: Keyboard Events
item.description:
Can we play yet?#

We can draw a rectangle. We can change its colour. We can even make it move across the screen.

Now imagine watching that rectangle move from left to right. Again. And again.

It might be interesting for a little while.

But there is nothing for us to do. Whatever we press, the rectangle continues with its very important rectangle business.

That gets boring.

Think about a game you enjoy. What would happen if you could no longer control anything? The player runs by itself, jumps by itself, and wins or loses without your help.

item.title: Drawing Text
item.description:
Drawing text#

We’ve spent a lot of time drawing things such as rectangles, circles and lines.

But what if we want to put some words on the screen?

Raylib provides DrawText for this.

The basic API looks like this:

r.DrawText("Hello, Raylib!", 20, 20, 24, r.WHITE);

The arguments are:

  1. The text to draw.
  2. The x-coordinate.
  3. The y-coordinate.
  4. The font size.
  5. The color.

For example:

r.DrawText("Hello", 50, 50, 20, r.WHITE);
r.DrawText("Raylib", 50, 80, 30, r.YELLOW);

The two pieces of text can have different positions, sizes and colors.

item.title: The Long Run
item.description:
The Long Run#

A dinosaur is running through an empty world.

It cannot stop. Cacti and birds appear in its path. It must jump over one and duck under the other.

We will build the game a little at a time. Each assignment adds something to the game you made in the previous one.

Do not jump into the code immediately. Read the assignment first and understand what the game should do.

item.title: Textures
item.description:
Additional Raylib API#

So far, we’ve learned how to draw a few basic shapes with Raylib.

We’ve also learned how to work with objects in Raylib, including Color and Vector2.

In this post, we’ll add a few more tools to our drawing vocabulary:

  • drawing onto a render texture

The goal here is simple: learn what these APIs let us do and get comfortable using them.

We will not try to understand everything happening inside Raylib. Where there is an interesting idea underneath an API, we’ll take a brief look at it.

item.title: Worldly Woes
item.description:
The Woes Of The World#

When we started writing Raylib programs, I gave you a template that used a world object.

The idea was simple. We needed a way to share information between setup(), update(), and draw(). So setup() would create a world, and the other functions would use it.

This was a reasonable idea.

Unfortunately, the world has grown in power. It now knows everything, goes everywhere, and is invited to functions that have absolutely no business meeting it.

item.title: Trigonometry
item.description:
Trigonometry Challenges#

You have spent some time with our trigonometry primer .

The primer was not meant to be a list of formulas for you to memorize. It was meant to give you a way of thinking about angles, circles, coordinates, sine, cosine, radians and polar coordinates.

Now we are going to use those ideas.

For each of the following challenges, write a small Raylib program. Each challenge is independent. You should be able to run each program by itself.

item.title: A World Tour
item.description:
A World Tour#

You’ve learned how to use loops. Now we’re going to use them to recreate a series of images with Raylib.

For each exercise, you will be given an image. Recreate the image using a loop.

The dimensions and number of strips in your program should be configurable.

1. Spain#

Recreate the image using Raylib.

  • The reference image is 440 × 440 pixels.
  • The dimensions of your drawing should be configurable.
  • The number of strips should be configurable.
  • The strips should have equal width.
  • Use r.RED and r.GOLD.
  • Repeat the pattern shown in the image.

2. Spanish Gap#

item.title: Objects in Raylib
item.description:
Objects in Raylib#

We have learned about objects in JavaScript.

So far, we have mostly looked at objects as a way of putting related information together:

const student = {
 name: "Ravi",
 age: 20,
};

The useful thing about this is not the curly braces. The useful thing is that we can give a shape to something we are thinking about.

Raylib has many things that naturally have more than one piece of information.

A colour has several components.

item.title: Particle Detector 2
item.description:
Extension — Scan in Two Directions#

Our particle detector has so far been scanning from left to right and back again.

That means we have been thinking about ranges along the horizontal direction.

But our region of space has two dimensions.

Why should we only scan horizontally?

A particle detector could also scan from top to bottom.

A New Direction#

Add another scanner to your simulation.

This scanner should move vertically.

item.title: Particle Detector
item.description:
Scanning for Particles#

Imagine that we have sent a particle detector into space.

The detector is looking at a small region of space around it. It moves from one side of the region to the other, scanning for particles as it goes.

Our job is to build a simulation of this detector.

You will build the simulation in several steps. Each step adds one small idea to the previous one.

item.title: Template
item.description:
Modules and a Raylib Template#

So far, each Raylib program you have written has lived in a single file.

We have already started organizing that file into functions:

function setup() {}

function update() {}

function draw() {}

function loop() {
 while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) {
 update();
 draw();
 }
}

function main() {
 setup();
 loop();
}

main();

This gives different parts of the program different responsibilities.

But there is another kind of organization available to us.

We can separate our program into different files.

item.title: Skeleton
item.description:
Organizing a Raylib Program#

You have now written a few small Raylib programs.

You have probably noticed that even a small program starts to contain several different kinds of code:

  • code that prepares the window
  • code that changes things
  • code that draws things
  • code that keeps the program running

It is useful to give these different responsibilities a little structure.

We are going to use the following skeleton:

function setup() {}

function update() {}

function draw() {}

function loop() {
 update();
 draw();
}

function main() {
 setup();
 loop();
}

main();

This is not a rule imposed by Raylib.

item.title: Simple exercises
item.description:
First Exercises#

You now have a working Raylib program.

You have seen how a Raylib program is structured, and you have used functions such as r.DrawRectangle.

Now it is time to start solving some small problems.

For these exercises, create a directory called:

workspace/raylib_exercises/

Each exercise should be its own program.

Use these filenames:

01_center_rectangle.js
02_center_rectangle_in_rectangle.js
03_scale_and_center.js
04_closer_target.js

Write the Raylib program yourself for each exercise. You should not need to copy the program from the previous post.

item.title: Raylib anatomy
item.description:
The anatomy of a Raylib program#

In the previous post, we saw that Raylib is a library that gives our JavaScript programs a collection of functions for working with graphics.

We are now going to look at a complete Raylib program.

Don’t worry if you don’t understand everything in it yet.

In fact, you shouldn’t.

Read through it once and see if you can recognize anything.

const r = require("raylib");

r.InitWindow(800, 400, "Raylib");
r.SetTargetFPS(60);

while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) {
 r.BeginDrawing();
 r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK);

 r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE);

 r.EndDrawing();
}

r.CloseWindow();

There are quite a few things happening here.

item.title: Intro to Graphics/Raylib
item.description:
Raylib#

So far, most of the programs you have written have produced things like numbers and text.

You might have written:

console.log(2 + 3);

and seen:

5

Or perhaps you wrote a function that takes some values, performs a computation, and returns another value.

What if the result of our program could be something that we could see?

What if instead of producing:

5

our program could produce a rectangle on the screen?

That is where we are going next.
